answer:
Short answer: plain containment will not carry the administrative history — but not for the reason the question supposes, and the remedy is not "each administrative unit as its own place with a bounded period". An instance of E53 Place cannot be bounded in time at all: E53 comprises extents in space "independent from temporal phenomena and matter" (crm732#E53). Places do not stop existing. What stopped existing in 1894 was the hundred, and the hundred is not a place. So the chain does get fuller, but the temporal bound sits on the *unit*, not on the place.

1) THE MILL. One instance of E22 Human-Made Object throughout, and nothing in this case touches it. Neither the rename nor the boundary reform is an E11 Modification, an E81 Transformation or an E12 Production, and none of what follows asserts a change to the structure.

2) THE NAMES. Attach both to the same E22 with P1 is identified by: E41 Appellation "Fen End Mill" and E41 Appellation "Bell's Mill". This is deliberately safe rather than sloppy, because P1 is by design time-neutral — its scope note states that it "does not reveal anything about when, where and by whom this identifier was used" (crm732#P1). Accumulating a second name is therefore monotonic, not a revision: "the CIDOC CRM always gives priority to modelling properties as time-neutral, and rather representing changes by events" (Modelling principles > Monotonicity, crm732#s0058). The same passage tells you where the dates go if you need them: "If a more specific temporal knowledge is required/available, it is recommended to explicitly describe the events leading to the assertion of that property for that item."

For the dates of use, the SIG settled this under Issue 147: "the scope of usage and the date of usage do not pertain to the names themselves but to activities dealing with the names" (issue147#background-s0000), and the resolution (Nuremberg 2007 / Heraklion 2008) was that no new class was needed — an example was added to E7 Activity and the name-use case was written into P16, whose scope note now covers "the use of a particular name by a particular group of people over some span to identify a thing" (crm732#P16). So: an E7 Activity per name-in-use, with P16 used specific object to the E41 Appellation, P4 has time-span to an E52 Time-Span (estate-map period; 1850s onward), and P14 carried out by if you can name the community or the estate office. E7's own example list carries the parallel case (the people of Iraq calling a place "Quyunjig"). Because the naming is an activity that merely *used* the name, it makes no claim about the mill's fabric.

3) THE ADMINISTRATIVE UNITS. Each is an instance of E4 Period, typed as hundred / rural district. The E4 scope note is explicit: "geopolitical units and activities of settlements are regarded as special cases of E4 Period" (crm732#E4), the geopolitical-unit paragraph having been drafted and closed under Issue 312 "Mapping Geopolitical Units to Period" (issue312#current-s0000). The list says the same in plainer words — Martin Doerr: "a geopolitical entity is indeed regarded as a case (type, specialization) of E4 Period" (t1090), and, refusing exactly the shortcut this case proposes, "All examples you gave of things with a political identity are instances of E4 Period" (t1243). In t1093, Richard Light's suggestion that an administrative unit be a subclass of E7 Activity was turned down on the ground that "not all things having a temporal dimension are activities".

So: Sedgewick Hundred (E4) P4 has time-span an E52 ending 1894; Whitgate Rural District (E4) P4 has time-span an E52 beginning 1894. Each unit P161 has spatial projection an E53 Place — "extent of Sedgewick Hundred", "extent of Whitgate Rural District" — and that is where a mapped boundary and its coordinates belong. The two extents survive 1894 untouched; only the periods are bounded. The succession can be stated with P132 spatiotemporally overlaps with between the two E4 Periods, or, if you want strict ordering, P182 ends before or with the start of.

4) THE MEMBERSHIP, TIME-BOUNDED. Two instances of E93 Presence, each a slice of the mill's own spacetime volume:
  - Presence A: P195 was a presence of → the mill; P164 is temporally specified by → E52 (18th century to 1894); P10 falls within → Sedgewick Hundred (E4).
  - Presence B: P195 was a presence of → the mill; P164 is temporally specified by → E52 (1894 onward); P10 falls within → Whitgate Rural District (E4).
P10 is the load-bearing link, and the specification's warning about it is this case in miniature: P10 "is the complete inclusion of one spacetime volume in another. It should not be confused with inclusion in the spatial and temporal projection, which may be larger. E.g., in 14 AD, Mesopotamia was not within the Roman Empire" (crm732#s0085). After 1894 the mill still stands on ground the hundred used to cover, yet it is not within the hundred — precisely the distinction a plain containment link destroys. If you would rather stay at the level of mapped extents, P167 was within → the E53 extent does the geometric half of the same job; it is declared as a shortcut of E93 Presence → P161 has spatial projection → E53 Place → P89 falls within → E53 Place, i.e. it is exactly P89 with a time-span bolted on, and it "may also be used to describe a confinement of the spatial extent of some realm during a known time-span" (crm732#P167).

5) WHAT PLAIN CONTAINMENT IS STILL GOOD FOR. Record the invariant the case cares about — same structure, same site — with P156 occupies from the mill to an E53 Place for the mill site, and, if you want the geometry, P89 falls within from that site to each unit's extent. Just do not read administrative membership off it. P89 "addresses spatial containment only and does not imply any relationship between things or phenomena occupying these places" (crm732#P89), and being reflexive and transitive it is true for all time or not at all.

One correction to the framing of the question: it is not the hundred's abolition that forces the fuller chain. Even had Sedgewick Hundred survived to today, P89 would still not say that the mill *belonged to* it, nor when. What forces the fuller chain is wanting a temporally qualified relationship at all; the abolition merely makes the loss visible, because the untimed geometric statement stays true after the thing it stands for has gone.

rejected_alternatives.option: E53 Place for Sedgewick Hundred and Whitgate Rural District (the plain-containment reading in the question)
rejected_alternatives.why_not: E53 is a purely geometric extent, 'independent from temporal phenomena and matter' (crm732#E53), so it can never be given the 1894 bound the case needs, and P89 between two such extents 'addresses spatial containment only and does not imply any relationship between things or phenomena occupying these places' (crm732#P89). Doerr rejected exactly this move in t1243. The unit is an E4 Period; its extent is the E53, reached by P161.

rejected_alternatives.option: E92 Spacetime Volume (bare) for the administrative units
rejected_alternatives.why_not: This was Dan Matei's proposal in t1243 — fiat territories as E92, bona fide places as E53 — and it was redirected: political entities are E4 Period, which already IsA E92 and so inherits P10, P132, P160, P161. A bare E92 loses the phenomenal identity (the governing activity) that makes 'Sedgewick Hundred' one thing rather than a chosen block of spacetime.

rejected_alternatives.option: E74 Group for the administrative units
rejected_alternatives.why_not: The Group is the body that governed — the district council or the hundred court — not the unit itself. Light ruled it out in the opening message of t1093, and the SIG routed geopolitical units to E4 Period instead (Issue 312, issue312#current-s0000). Modelling the unit as a Group would also mis-locate its spatial extent, since a Group has residences (P74), not spatial projections.

rejected_alternatives.option: E7 Activity for the administrative units
rejected_alternatives.why_not: Light's own first proposal in t1093, on the grounds that administrative units have a temporal dimension. Doerr answered that 'not all things having a temporal dimension are activities' and that results of activities are not activities. E4 Period is the right level: it covers the whole set of coherent phenomena of belonging to a jurisdictional area, not a single intentional action.
P99 dissolved has range E74 Group, so E68 can only end an actor, not a period. The hundred's end is stated by the end of the E52 Time-Span on its E4 Period, plus P132 / P182 against the successor.

rejected_alternatives.option: E15 Identifier Assignment for the two names
rejected_alternatives.why_not: It is the standard's own fully developed path behind P1 (crm732#P1), and it would be right if the HER treated the map and census names as identifiers allocated in an identification system — P37/P38 range E42 Identifier. But nobody assigned 'Bell's Mill'; it came into use. Issue 147 puts date-of-usage on activities dealing with the names, and P16's scope note was amended precisely for names used by a group over a span, so E7 Activity + P16 fits the evidence (estate maps, census returns) better here.

rejected_alternatives.option: E11 Modification or E81 Transformation for either change
rejected_alternatives.why_not: Both assert an intervention on the fabric. The case is explicit that the structure and the site are unchanged; the rename and the boundary reform must leave the E22 and its spacetime volume untouched, which is why every construct above is either time-neutral (P1, P156, P89) or a slice of the mill's existing volume (E93).

siblings_considered.why_not: E25 Human-Made Feature (like E22, a subclass of E24) covers features with 'no natural borders that separate them completely in an objective way from the carrier objects' — scratches, rock-cut chambers, canals. A windmill is a bounded structure that is a unit of documentation in its own right, so E22 holds. The SIG has never settled where immobile built structures sit on this boundary (t0821, t1874), but nothing in this case turns on it: E93 Presence, P196/P156 and P89 are all declared at or above E18.

E73 Information Object, the other subclass of E90 Symbolic Object, is for items with an objectively recognisable structure documented as single units — texts, images, datasets — which identify by their content. 'Fen End Mill' and 'Bell's Mill' identify 'by convention, tradition, or agreement', which is the E41 criterion. (If the HER wants the language of the names, the CRM's advice is to declare the same instances as E33 Linguistic Object too, not to swap E41 for E73.)

E63 Beginning of Existence, a sibling of E7 under E5 Event, would say the naming brought something into existence — which is the very implication the case forbids. 'Bell's Mill' coming into use started no mill and ended none; the E7 merely used a name over a span, via P16.

E93 Presence, the other subclass of E92, is a time-slice whose temporal extent is 'chosen in order to determine the spatial extent of a phenomenon'. Sedgewick Hundred is the phenomenon, not a slice of one: it has its own coherence (the jurisdiction and its administration) and its own real end in 1894. Using E93 for the hundred would make its 1894 boundary an artefact of the researcher's chosen window rather than a historical fact.

The mill's whereabouts from the eighteenth century to 1894 is not a set of coherent phenomena with an identity of its own — it is a cut we make through the mill's spacetime volume in order to state where it was then, which is exactly E93's job. Calling it an E4 Period would invent a historical phenomenon ('the mill's Sedgewick era') that no source attests and that would then need its own participants and causal parts (P9).

E92 Spacetime Volume, a sibling of E53 under E1, is what we deliberately keep out of the mapped boundary. The extent of Sedgewick Hundred has to be the timeless geometric object that P161 projects onto and that P89 relates to other extents; putting time back into it would collapse the very distinction (unit vs. extent) that lets the hundred end in 1894 while its boundary stays available for mapping.

E2 Temporal Entity, a sibling of E52 under E1, is the phenomenon that happens over a span; E52 is the span itself, with 'no semantic connotations about phenomena happening within the temporal extent'. '1894' and 'the 1850s onward' are positions on the timeline that qualify the units and the presences — the phenomena are already modelled as the E4 Periods and E7 Activities that carry them via P4.

notes: Two friction points. (a) search.py quote will not take a class or property id as a source — 'quote P89 ...' returns UNKNOWN SOURCE. Scope-note quotes have to be aimed at the declaration chunk (crm732#P89), whose id is only discoverable by running docs --kind declaration --json; concept <id> prints the scope note but not the chunk id you need to verify a phrase from it. (b) docs snippets truncate at roughly 250 characters, so the decisive passages (Modelling principles > Monotonicity, and the Spatiotemporal Relations section) were only readable via --json. Also worth flagging: the episode summary for t1019 is labelled 'Modeling populated places with temporal and spatial variation using sp...' but the thread is actually about End of Existence for E30 Right — a wasted read. On substance, the one point I could not close from the tools is whether an immobile built structure should be E22 or E25; the SIG discussed it in t0821 and again in t1874 (December 2025) without reaching a decision, so I took E22 and noted that nothing in the recommended pattern depends on the choice.
